title: Pope Leo XIV Draws 700,000 to Paris Mass, Praises Youth as 'Today's Church'
summary: An estimated 700,000 people filled the Place de la Concorde in Paris on Saturday for an open-air Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV — one of the largest crowds of his four-day visit to France. The event began with the pontiff riding down the Champs-Élysées Avenue in his open-topped popemobile, waving to crowds and blessing children. In his homily, the Pope urged Catholics not to keep their faith private. "Let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed," he said. He reserved special words for young people, calling them "today's Church." "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said. On Friday, he had joined 80,000 young people at the Stade de France. French President Emmanuel Macron met the Pope on Friday but did not attend Saturday's Mass — a deliberate choice to respect France's strict separation of church and state. His wife, Brigitte Macron, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu did attend, along with several candidates for next year's presidential election, including Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally and centrists Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal. Earlier Saturday, the Pope visited the Maison Bakhita center, which supports refugees, praising it for inviting people "to see those who are invisible." He also stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love" and warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence. Large crowds are expected for the rest of his trip, which the Church sees as a sign of growing spirituality in France and Europe. The Pope's visit has drawn attention across the country, with many watching his message of faith and unity. His words to young people and his call to welcome refugees have sparked conversations about the role of the Church in modern society. As his trip continues, the excitement and turnout suggest a renewed interest in spirituality among many in France and beyond.
why_it_matters: The event puts the relationship between religion, politics and public life on display in a country that legally separates them, and it tests whether a huge, highly visible church moment can reverse decades of declining religious practice among young Europeans.

background_read: France has a strict rule called laïcité — the separation of church and state — which dates back to a 1905 law. It means the government stays neutral about religion, which is why President Emmanuel Macron (France's president since 2017) deliberately skipped the Mass even though his wife Brigitte and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu attended.

The Place de la Concorde (a huge public square in central Paris) and the Champs-Élysées (the city's famous main avenue leading to the Arc de Triomphe) are both symbols of national life, so holding a religious event there is politically significant.

Popes have drawn enormous crowds in France before: Pope John Paul II visited Paris in 1980 and returned in 1997 for World Youth Day, a global gathering of young Catholics. The National Rally (a French far-right party long associated with the Le Pen family) and rival parties are already campaigning for the next presidential election, which explains why so many politicians appeared at the event.

The Catholic Church in France, as in much of Western Europe, has seen attendance fall for decades, so a crowd of this size is being read by church leaders as a possible sign of renewed interest in spirituality — though big one-off events do not always translate into lasting change.

perspectives.description: Supporters see the 700,000-strong crowd and the 80,000 young people at the Stade de France as proof of renewed spiritual energy in a country where faith has faded. The Pope's praise for the refugee center and his focus on young people is framed as a welcoming, outward-looking message.

Some in France argue that a mass religious event in a national square, attended by leading politicians and election candidates, blurs the laïcité line the country guards carefully. Macron's absence was itself a statement that the state should not be seen endorsing a faith.

Big papal events have drawn huge crowds before, yet regular church attendance in France and Western Europe has kept falling for decades. Analysts caution that a spectacle-sized turnout signals visibility more than it proves a durable change in belief or practice.

The real test comes after the popemobile leaves: whether young Catholics stay engaged, whether the Church's message on refugees and women's roles shifts its image, and how it handles new questions like artificial intelligence. Politicians who attended may also find the visit shaping the tone of next year's election campaign.
